sources.entry: Auto-Vectorization in LLVM - Where LLVM lists what its loop and SLP vectorisers accept: interleaving, reductions, if-conversion and runtime checks.

summary.title: Auto-Vectorization in LLVM
summary.one_liner: LLVM's Loop Vectorizer and SLP Vectorizer: what loop shapes they accept (runtime checks, reductions, if-conversion, induction variables, scatter/gather, math calls), how to force widths and unroll factors, and how to diagnose missed vectorization with optimization remarks.
takeaways: LLVM has two vectorizers, both enabled by default: the Loop Vectorizer (loops) and the SLP Vectorizer (merges similar scalar instructions).
Vector width and interleave/unroll factors can be forced with -force-vector-width and -force-vector-interleave, or hinted per loop with #pragma clang loop.
Use -Rpass=loop-vectorize, -Rpass-missed and -Rpass-analysis to find which loops were skipped and why (e.g. a switch statement).
Floating-point reductions are vectorized only under reassociation-permitting flags such as -fassociative-math -fno-signed-zeros -fno-trapping-math on most targets.
summary.summary: The page is the LLVM documentation on its auto-vectorizers. It explains the Loop Vectorizer and SLP Vectorizer, how to disable them, and how to force vector width and unroll factors via command-line flags or clang loop pragmas. It then lists supported loop features with small C examples: unknown trip counts, runtime pointer checks, reductions, inductions, if-conversion, pointer induction, reverse loops, scatter/gather, mixed types, and math intrinsics. It also covers diagnostics with optimization remarks, epilogue and early-exit vectorization, and a short performance note.
